paragraphs.heading: What it is
paragraphs.text: Regression toward the mean, also called reversion to the mean or reversion to mediocrity, describes a pattern: when one draw of a random variable comes out extreme, the following draw of that same variable is likely to sit closer to its mean. It also covers a related case: sample a lot of random variables, then deliberately pick out the most extreme results. In many cases, sampling those picked-out variables a second time gives less extreme results, nearer the original mean of the whole group.

paragraphs.heading: When the effect is strong
paragraphs.text: How strong the effect is depends on whether all the variables come from the same distribution, or whether there are genuine differences between them. If they share one distribution, the effect is statistically likely. If they truly differ, it may be weaker or absent.

paragraphs.heading: A test of pure guessing
paragraphs.text: Picture a class taking a 100-question true/false test where every student guesses at random on every question. Each score is then a random draw with an expected mean of 50, though by chance some students land well above 50 and some well below. Take only the top 10% and give them a second test, again guessing randomly, and their mean is expected to be near 50 again. Whatever a student scored the first time, the best prediction for the second test is 50.

paragraphs.heading: Skill mixed with luck
paragraphs.text: If there were no luck or guessing at all, each student would be expected to get the same score on a retest, and there would be no regression. Most real situations lie in between, with exam scores reflecting both skill and luck. The students above average then include skilled ones without especially bad luck, plus unskilled ones who were extremely lucky. On a retest, the unskilled are unlikely to be that lucky again, while the skilled get a fresh chance of bad luck.

paragraphs.heading: Everyday examples
paragraphs.text: A business with a highly profitable quarter, with no change in the underlying reasons for its performance, is likely to do less well the next quarter. Baseball players who hit well as rookies tend to do worse in their second season, the so-called sophomore slump. Regression toward the mean also explains the Sports Illustrated cover jinx. A spell of exceptional performance earns a cover, more ordinary performance follows, and it looks as if the cover caused the decline.

paragraphs.heading: Galton and heights
paragraphs.text: The idea has its roots in genetics, and Sir Francis Galton made it widely known in the late 19th century. Galton noticed that extreme traits in parents, such as height, are not fully passed on to their children, whose traits drift back toward a middle point now identified as the mean. By measuring the heights of hundreds of people, he estimated the size of the effect. For height he put the coefficient at about 2/3, so a person's height tends to fall around a midpoint set at two thirds of how far the parents stand from the average.
